overview.title: Finishing the Sequential walkthrough; introducing the Functional API
overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: The end of the incremental-summary debugging workflow for Sequential models, the limitations of Sequential, and a first Functional-API model (Listing 7.8).
overview.central_idea: Sequential models only express single-input, single-output linear stacks; real models often need multiple inputs, multiple outputs or non-linear topologies, so most Keras models use the Functional API, in which you declare an Input, call layers on it, and wrap inputs and outputs in keras.Model.
overview.importance: This is the start of the most commonly used model-building API in the book. Listing 7.8 is the template every later Functional model follows.
learning_objectives: Explain why tracking summary() after each add() is useful for shape-transforming layers.
List the three things the Sequential model cannot express (multiple inputs, multiple outputs, non-linear topology).

See that Listing 7.8 is the same two-layer stack as Listings 7.1-7.7.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Printing summary() after each added layer is a common debugging workflow for layers that transform inputs in complex ways, such as convolutional layers (chapter 8).
paragraphs.what_it_means: For Dense layers, output shapes are trivial (None, units). For convolution or pooling layers, output shapes depend on kernel size, strides and padding, so checking them incrementally catches mistakes early.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: You will use exactly this habit when building convnets in chapter 8.

paragraphs.excerpt: The Sequential model is easy to use, but its applicability is extremely
paragraphs.what_it_says: Sequential can only express single-input, single-output models applying layers one after another, while real models often have multiple inputs, multiple outputs or nonlinear topology.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The three examples correspond to three graph features: a node with several sources (multi-input), several sinks (multi-output), and branches/merges in between (nonlinear topology, e.g. residual connections).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the precise test for when to leave Sequential: if any of the three applies, you need the Functional API (or subclassing).

concepts.name: Functional API
concepts.definition: Keras API in which a model is defined by calling layers on symbolic input tensors and passing the resulting inputs and outputs to keras.Model.
concepts.intuition: LEGO bricks: each layer call snaps a new brick onto existing ones.
concepts.technical: inputs = keras.Input(...); x = Layer(...)(inputs); ...; model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs). The model is a DAG of layers.
concepts.significance: Handles multiple inputs/outputs and nonlinear topologies; used by most Keras models in the wild.
concepts.misconception: That it is only for complex models; it expresses simple stacks too.

concepts.name: Sequential model
concepts.definition: An ordered stack of layers with one input and one output.
concepts.technical: Cannot express multiple inputs, multiple outputs or nonlinear topology.
concepts.misconception: That Sequential limits depth; it limits topology.

concepts.name: Nonlinear topology
concepts.definition: A model graph that is not a single chain of layers.
concepts.intuition: Roads that fork and merge rather than one straight road.
concepts.technical: Graph property: some layer has more than one input or its output feeds more than one layer.
concepts.significance: One of the three reasons to use the Functional API.
concepts.example: Beyond the book: residual connections add a layer's input to its output.
concepts.misconception: Confusing it with nonlinear activation functions.

code.title: A simple Functional model with two Dense layers
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(3,), name="my_input")
features = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")(inputs)
outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)
model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs, name="my_functional_model")
code.what_it_does: Defines the two-layer stack with the Functional API: Input → Dense(64, relu) → Dense(10, softmax), wrapped in a named keras.Model.

Create and call a Dense(10, softmax) layer on features; 'outputs' has shape (None, 10).
Instantiate a Model by specifying which tensors are inputs and outputs; Keras traces the graph between them.

deeper.title: Sequential vs Functional, side by side
deeper.body:
Same model, two styles (Listing 7.7 continued vs Listing 7.8):

- Sequential: `model.add(keras.Input(shape=(3,)))`, `model.add(Dense(64, ...))`, `model.add(Dense(10, ...))` — the wiring is implicit (list order).
- Functional: each layer call names its input explicitly: `Dense(64)(inputs)`, `Dense(10)(features)`, and the model is defined by `inputs` and `outputs`.

Note (AI explanation): because the wiring is explicit, nothing stops you from calling a layer on *two* tensors' concatenation, or using `features` twice — exactly what Sequential can't express.

deeper.title: The three limitations as graph shapes
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: think of a model as a graph of layers.

- **Multiple inputs** = more than one source node (image branch + metadata branch merging).
- **Multiple outputs** = more than one sink node (e.g. a priority score and a department label).
- **Nonlinear topology** = branches and merges in the middle (e.g. skip connections).

A Sequential model is the special case of a graph that is a single path.

misconceptions.claim: 'Nonlinear topology' means the model uses nonlinear activations.
misconceptions.correction: It refers to the graph shape — branches, merges, multiple paths — not activation functions; Listing 7.1 has relu but a linear (chain) topology.

misconceptions.claim: The Functional API is only for multi-input or multi-output models.
misconceptions.correction: Listing 7.8 uses it for a plain two-layer stack; it is the general-purpose API.

misconceptions.claim: In Listing 7.8, Dense(64, activation="relu")(inputs) computes on real data.
misconceptions.correction: inputs is a symbolic tensor; the call returns another symbolic tensor describing shape and dtype (p.220).

takeaways: Incremental summary() checks are a common debugging tool, especially for convolutional layers (chapter 8).
Sequential models are limited to one input, one output, and a linear chain of layers.
Multiple inputs, multiple outputs, or nonlinear topology call for the Functional API.
Most Keras models in the wild use the Functional API.
Functional pattern: Input → call layers on tensors → keras.Model(inputs, outputs).

questions.question: Which of the following can a Sequential model express?
options: A model taking an image and its metadata
A model predicting two different things about the data
A 20-layer stack of Dense layers with one input and one output
A model with a branch that merges back later
questions.answer: A 20-layer stack of Dense layers with one input and one output
questions.explanation: Sequential is limited to single input, single output, one layer after another; depth is not restricted. The other three are the page's examples of multiple inputs, multiple outputs and nonlinear topology.

questions.question: In Listing 7.8, what are the two arguments that define the model's graph in keras.Model?
questions.explanation: Keras traces the layers connecting these symbolic tensors.

questions.question: Why does the page say incremental summary() checks are common for convolutional layers?
questions.answer: Because such layers transform their inputs' shapes in complex ways, so tracking the output shape after each layer helps debugging.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after the summary.

questions.question: How many parameters does the model in Listing 7.8 have?
questions.explanation: Same layers and input size as the Sequential version: 3·64+64 = 256 plus 64·10+10 = 650.

questions.question: What does 'nonlinear topology' mean in this section, and why can't a Python list represent it?
questions.answer: A layer graph with branches, merges or multiple paths. A list gives each layer exactly one predecessor and one successor, so it can only express a single chain.
questions.explanation: The book names nonlinear topology as a Sequential limitation; the list argument follows from p.216's 'basically a Python list'.
